method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 7 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 10 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 77 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 50 USD. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 8,000 USD: 7,667 of 10,000, which is 77%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

choice: We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
The behaviour check kept the 12 that fit how you take risk.

Each of those 12 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. The best chance among them was 77%. 10 portfolios were within 1 percentage point of it, too close for the simulation to tell apart, so we chose the one of those that falls least short in the worst 5 of every 100 futures (77% chance).
disclosures: IMPORTANT: The projections or other information in this section regarding the likelihood of various investment outcomes are hypothetical in nature, do not reflect actual investment results and are not guarantees of future results.
Results may vary with each use and over time: new market data, a change to your goal, your monthly amount, your time horizon or the funds available can all change them.
The simulation replays past market behaviour. The future can be worse than anything in the history used, and the simulation cannot show events that history does not contain.

Assumed: the monthly amount is paid in (or taken out) every month as planned, the portfolio is rebalanced back to its mix every month, and today's fund fees apply. Not included: taxes, inflation (amounts are in future dollars), trading costs after the first purchase, and changes you make along the way.
A high chance is not a promise and a low chance is not a certainty of failure. Review the plan when your situation or the markets change.

Your goal: 8,000 USD in 10 years

Hypothetical simulation based on past market data; not a forecast. You start with 500 USD, add 50 USD every month, and want 8,000 USD in 10 years. Paid in without any growth: 6,500 USD.

77%

In about 77 of every 100 simulated futures, this portfolio reaches your goal of 8,000 USD or more in 10 years. In the other 23 it falls short.

Reach the goal (77)Fall short (23)

With 10,000 simulated futures the simulation's own error is about ±1 percentage point, so the chance is shown rounded. Which years history happens to contain matters far more: drawing only from 2007 to 2017 gives 50%, only from 2017 to 2026 gives 92%. Read the chance as a rough guide, not an exact figure.

  • In the worst 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with less than 7,120 USD.
  • Half of the simulated futures end above 9,340 USD and half below. This middle outcome is not a promise, and not more likely than the amounts around it.
  • In the best 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with more than 12,300 USD.

How bad could a miss be?

  • If it goes badly: 2,040 USD short. In the worst 5 of every 100 simulated futures you would end, on average, 2,040 USD short of your goal.
  • Falls along the way: -12% typical. Along the way, the account falls at some point by about 12% from its previous high in a typical future, and by 21% or more in 1 in 10. About 12 in 100 futures see a fall of 20% or more.

What would change your odds

Each line changes ONE thing and re-runs the same simulated futures with the same portfolio, so the difference comes only from that change.

ChangeChance
Your plan as it is77%
Add 60 USD a month instead of 50 USD93%
Give it 2 years more (12 years in total)95%
Give it 5 years more (15 years in total)more than 99%
Aim for 7,120 USD instead of 8,000 USD90%

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 7 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 10 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 77 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 50 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 8,000 USD: 7,667 of 10,000, which is 77%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How this portfolio was chosen

  • We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
  • The behaviour check kept the 12 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 12 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. The best chance among them was 77%. 10 portfolios were within 1 percentage point of it, too close for the simulation to tell apart, so we chose the one of those that falls least short in the worst 5 of every 100 futures (77% chance).

About these numbers

  • IMPORTANT: The projections or other information in this section regarding the likelihood of various investment outcomes are hypothetical in nature, do not reflect actual investment results and are not guarantees of future results.
  • Results may vary with each use and over time: new market data, a change to your goal, your monthly amount, your time horizon or the funds available can all change them.
  • The simulation replays past market behaviour. The future can be worse than anything in the history used, and the simulation cannot show events that history does not contain.
  • Assumed: the monthly amount is paid in (or taken out) every month as planned, the portfolio is rebalanced back to its mix every month, and today's fund fees apply. Not included: taxes, inflation (amounts are in future dollars), trading costs after the first purchase, and changes you make along the way.
  • A high chance is not a promise and a low chance is not a certainty of failure. Review the plan when your situation or the markets change.

Why this portfolio

  • Your answers placed you in category C4 (C1 is the most cautious, C5 the most growth-oriented). That category aims for about 60% in stocks and sets hard limits of at most 70% in stocks, 15% in gold and commodities, 0% in crypto, 13% volatility and a 35% loss in one specific test: equities fall 30%, bonds 5%, gold and commodities 15%, crypto 60%.
  • Your category rests on three things: your answers on attitude to risk (level 4 of 5, two thirds), the Risk Game you played (level 4 of 5, one third) and your finances (a cap at level 4). Your attitude to risk came to level 4; your category is the lower of that and the cap: C4.
  • We built 100 different portfolios inside your limits. The behaviour check kept 12 that fit how you take risk, and we chose the one with the highest chance of reaching your goal (77%) in a simulation on past market data. That chance is hypothetical, not a forecast.
  • Market volatility is currently low (recent volatility is 0.71 times its long-run level), so no extra reduction of the risk budget was needed.
  • The portfolio holds 7 funds, equivalent to about 6.9 equally sized holdings. Its volatility is 8% lower than if every holding moved in step with the others.

Where the risk comes from

A holding can be a small part of your money and a large part of your risk. This compares each holding's share of the money with its share of the portfolio's risk.

Share of moneyShare of risk

Historical estimates: a bad single day (1-in-20) lost about 0.9% or more; the average of the worst days lost 1.2%; the largest fall from peak to bottom in the data window was 6.6%. If all markets moved together more than usual, volatility could reach 9.7%.

Put the other way round: stock markets would have to fall about 56% (with everything else unchanged) before this portfolio reached the loss limit you set.

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 4 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 11 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future

method.title: Counting the futures

method.title: The same futures for every option

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 4 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 1 year. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 11 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add nothing more. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 84,000 USD: 4,810 of 10,000, which is 48%.
  6. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How this portfolio was chosen

  • We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
  • The behaviour check kept the 5 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 5 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. The best chance among them was 48%. 4 portfolios were within 1 percentage point of it, too close for the simulation to tell apart, so we chose the one of those that falls least short in the worst 5 of every 100 futures (48% chance).

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 13 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 500 USD. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 400,000 USD: 8,407 of 10,000, which is 84%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (7 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 13 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 500 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 400,000 USD: 8,407 of 10,000, which is 84%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (7 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 36 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 8 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 69 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 200 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 60,000 USD: 6,612 of 10,000, which is 66%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (30 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (13 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How this portfolio was chosen

  • We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
  • The behaviour check kept the 5 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 5 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. The best chance among them was 66%. 2 portfolios were within 1 percentage point of it, too close for the simulation to tell apart, so we chose the one of those that falls least short in the worst 5 of every 100 futures (66% chance).

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 42 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 12 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 83 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 300 USD. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 120,000 USD: 9,196 of 10,000, which is 92%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (47 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (6 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 300 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 120,000 USD: 9,196 of 10,000, which is 92%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (47 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). Investments younger than the history used (6 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 77 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Counting the futures

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up.   5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 180,000 USD: 3,894 of 10,000, which is 39%.

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 5 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 700 USD. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 160,000 USD: 10,000 of 10,000, which is 100%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How bad could a miss be?

  • If it goes badly: Goal still reached. Even in the worst 5 of every 100 simulated futures you would reach your goal.
  • Falls along the way: -7% typical. Along the way, the account falls at some point by about 7% from its previous high in a typical future, and by 11% or more in 1 in 10. About 1 in 100 futures see a fall of 20% or more.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 5 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 700 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 160,000 USD: 10,000 of 10,000, which is 100%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How this portfolio was chosen

  • We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
  • The behaviour check kept the 20 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 20 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. The best chance among them was 100%. 20 portfolios were within 1 percentage point of it, too close for the simulation to tell apart, so we chose the one of those that falls least short in the worst 5 of every 100 futures (100% chance).

Where the risk comes from

A holding can be a small part of your money and a large part of your risk. This compares each holding's share of the money with its share of the portfolio's risk.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 5 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 700 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 160,000 USD: 10,000 of 10,000, which is 100%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

  • The behaviour check kept the 20 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 20 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. Where the risk comes from

A holding can be a small part of your money and a large part of your risk. This compares each holding's share of the money with its share of the portfolio's risk.

Share of moneyShare of risk

Historical estimates: a bad single day (1-in-20) lost about 0.6% or more; the average of the worst days lost 0.7%; the largest fall from peak to bottom in the data window was 3.6%. If all markets moved together more than usual, volatility could reach 5.6%.

We built a range of portfolios from cautious to bolder, each with the lowest volatility we could find for its share of stocks. More stocks means more risk. The 'simple mix' is a naive split with no optimisation.

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 9 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 8 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 69 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add nothing more. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 70,000 USD: 4,328 of 10,000, which is 43%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

choice: We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
The behaviour check kept the 20 that fit how you take risk.
Each of those 20 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. This portfolio had the highest chance of reaching your goal: 43%.
disclosures: IMPORTANT: The projections or other information in this section regarding the likelihood of various investment outcomes are hypothetical in nature, do not reflect actual investment results and are not guarantees of future results.
Results may vary with each use and over time: new market data, a change to your goal, your monthly amount, your time horizon or the funds available can all change them.
The simulation replays past market behaviour. The future can be worse than anything in the history used, and the simulation cannot show events that history does not contain.

Your goal: 70,000 USD in 8 years

Hypothetical simulation based on past market data; not a forecast. You start with 40,000 USD, add nothing more, and want 70,000 USD in 8 years. Paid in without any growth: 40,000 USD.

43%

In about 43 of every 100 simulated futures, this portfolio reaches your goal of 70,000 USD or more in 8 years. In the other 57 it falls short.

Reach the goal (43)Fall short (57)

With 10,000 simulated futures the simulation's own error is about ±1 percentage point, so the chance is shown rounded. Which years history happens to contain matters far more: drawing only from 2007 to 2017 gives 24%, only from 2017 to 2026 gives 64%. Read the chance as a rough guide, not an exact figure.

Where you could end up

  • In the worst 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with less than 50,900 USD.
  • Half of the simulated futures end above 67,500 USD and half below. This middle outcome is not a promise, and not more likely than the amounts around it.
  • In the best 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with more than 89,200 USD.

How bad could a miss be?

  • If it goes badly: 27,400 USD short. In the worst 5 of every 100 simulated futures you would end, on average, 27,400 USD short of your goal.
  • Falls along the way: -11% typical. Along the way, the account falls at some point by about 11% from its previous high in a typical future, and by 19% or more in 1 in 10. About 8 in 100 futures see a fall of 20% or more.

What would change your odds

Each line changes ONE thing and re-runs the same simulated futures with the same portfolio, so the difference comes only from that change.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 9 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 8 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 69 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add nothing more. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 70,000 USD: 4,328 of 10,000, which is 43%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (3 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (3 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

How this portfolio was chosen

  • We built 100 different portfolios, every one inside your limits.
  • The behaviour check kept the 20 that fit how you take risk.
  • Each of those 20 was simulated against your goal on the same futures. This portfolio had the highest chance of reaching your goal: 43%.

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 70 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 15 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 89 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.

method.title: Your plan in each future
method.text: Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add nothing more. Money cannot go below zero.

method.title: Counting the futures
method.text: We count the futures that end at or above 200,000 USD: 6,027 of 10,000, which is 60%.

method.title: Corrections against over-optimism
method.text: Stocks, stock funds and crypto-assets (65 in this simulation) are picked from today's most traded list, so their past returns flatter them (survivorship bias). We kept their real ups and downs but set their average return to what their sensitivity to the world stock market earned (beta times the market's average). Investments younger than the history used (10 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.

method.title: The same futures for every option
method.text: Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Investments younger than the history used (10 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

method.title: Market history
method.text: We took the real daily price changes of the 5 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.

method.title: 10,000 possible futures
method.text: Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 10 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.

method.title: Market regimes
method.text: A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. In about 99 of every 100 simulated futures, this portfolio reaches your goal of 110,000 USD or more in 10 years. In the other 1 it falls short.

With 10,000 simulated futures the simulation's own error is about ±1 percentage point, so the chance is shown rounded. Which years history happens to contain matters far more: drawing only from 2007 to 2017 gives more than 99%, only from 2017 to 2026 gives more than 99%. Read the chance as a rough guide, not an exact figure.

  • In the worst 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with less than 144,000 USD.
  • Half of the simulated futures end above 168,000 USD and half below. This middle outcome is not a promise, and not more likely than the amounts around it.
  • In the best 1 in 10 simulated futures you would end with more than 196,000 USD.

How bad could a miss be?

  • If it goes badly: 0 USD short. In the worst 5 of every 100 simulated futures you would end, on average, 0 USD short of your goal.
  • Falls along the way: -4% typical. Along the way, the account falls at some point by about 4% from its previous high in a typical future, and by 6% or more in 1 in 10. None of the simulated futures sees a fall of 20% or more.

How we calculated this

  1. Market history. We took the real daily price changes of the 5 investments in this portfolio from 2007-05-31 to 2026-10-16 (about 19 years, 4,877 trading days), a period that includes the 2008-09 financial crisis, the 2020 COVID crash and the 2022 fall of stocks and bonds together.
  2. 10,000 possible futures. Each simulated future is built month by month: we pick a random stretch of 21 consecutive trading days (about one month) from that history, then another, and so on for 10 years. Whole months keep crashes and rebounds together, the way they really happened.
  3. Market regimes. A machine-learning model (a Hidden Markov Model fitted on the daily returns and volatility of the S&P 500 fund SPY and the US bond fund AGG, 2007 to 2026) sorts every past trading day into one of four market regimes: calm, normal, stressed or crisis. Each simulated future moves from regime to regime month by month with the chances the model learned, and each month is drawn only from past months that began in the same regime, so a crisis lasts as long as crises really did instead of being broken up. Market regime today: normal (probability 98%). In about 77 of every 100 simulated futures, there is at least one crisis period lasting 3 months or more.
  4. Your plan in each future. Each month the portfolio earns that month's returns (rebalanced back to its mix), pays its fund fees, and then you add 300 USD. Money cannot go below zero.
  5. Counting the futures. We count the futures that end at or above 110,000 USD: 9,998 of 10,000, which is more than 99%.
  6. Corrections against over-optimism. Investments younger than the history used (1 in this simulation) had their missing early years rebuilt from the long-history funds they move with, adding no extra return.
  7. The same futures for every option. Every shortlisted portfolio was tested on exactly the same 10,000 futures (fixed random seed 20261017), so differences come from the portfolios, not from luck, and the same inputs always give the same result.

A holding can be a small part of your money and a large part of your risk. This compares each holding's share of the money with its share of the portfolio's risk.

Share of moneyShare of risk

Historical estimates: a bad single day (1-in-20) lost about 0.3% or more; the average of the worst days lost 0.5%; the largest fall from peak to bottom in the data window was 3.9%. If all markets moved together more than usual, volatility could reach 3.3%.

Assumptions and important information

  • Past data does not predict the future. Volatility and drawdown figures are estimates from recent history and can be wrong.
  • Stress scenarios are hypothetical shocks chosen in advance. They are not forecasts, and real losses can be larger.
  • This engine makes no forecast of returns. It is designed to control risk within your limits, not to promise gains.
  • Fund fees are shown as annual percentages. Trading costs are estimates and apply only to the first purchase or to changes.
  • Risk estimates use a standard statistical method (Ledoit-Wolf) over about 252 trading days.
  • Volatility is the typical size of the portfolio's yearly ups and downs. Stress scenario is a made-up market shock used to test the portfolio. Risk share is the part of total portfolio variance a holding is responsible for.
